title: Lighting Up Living Chemistry With PET
endLine: PET maps living chemistry with radioactive tracers, not clinical benefit.

scenes.tts: How can you watch chemistry happen inside a living body without opening it? Positron emission tomography, or PET, tracks radioactive tracers to map activity inside living tissue.
scenes.caption: How can you watch chemistry happen inside a living body without opening it? Positron emission tomography, or PET, tracks radioactive tracers to map activity inside living tissue.
scenes.visual: Dark frame with a clean human torso-and-brain silhouette (schematic) on the left glowing faintly inside; on the right, a linked circular zoom window shows one living cell (schematic, no molecular structures) as glowing tracer dots enter and illuminate the matching spot on the body.
scenes.narration: How can you watch chemistry happen inside a living body without opening it? Positron emission tomography, or PET, tracks radioactive tracers to map activity inside living tissue.

scenes.visual: The same living-body silhouette (schematic) stays softly glowing on the left while the title 'Lighting Up Living Chemistry With PET' fades in at full contrast for 1.5 seconds and clears.

scenes.tts: Zoom into one cell to see the classic scan's trick. In glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose, step one is a trap. The enzyme hexokinase moves a phosphate from A T P onto glucose. That phosphate's negative charge traps glucose inside the cell.
scenes.caption: Zoom into one cell to see the classic scan's trick. In glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose, step 1 is a trap. The enzyme hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP onto glucose. That phosphate's negative charge traps glucose inside the cell.
scenes.visual: Right zoomed cell window (schematic, no molecular structures): a glucose token enters; a clamshell hexokinase pocket closes around it and transfers a glowing minus-charge phosphate tag from an ATP token onto the glucose token (tag labelled 'carbon 6'). The negatively charged token bounces off the inner membrane wall, trapped.
scenes.narration: Zoom into one cell to see the classic scan's trick. In glycolysis, the breakdown of glucose, step 1 is a trap. The enzyme hexokinase moves a phosphate from ATP onto glucose. That phosphate's negative charge traps glucose inside the cell.

scenes.tts: F D G PET uses a glucose look-alike, or analog, labeled with radioactive fluorine eighteen. It is trapped after step one, and the scanner detects its radiation. So tissues taking up glucose fast light up. Many tumors take up glucose fast even with oxygen present, the Warburg effect.
scenes.caption: FDG-PET uses a glucose look-alike, or analog, labeled with radioactive fluorine-18. It is trapped after step 1, and the scanner detects its radiation. So tissues taking up glucose fast light up. Many tumors take up glucose fast even with oxygen present, the Warburg effect.
scenes.visual: Same zoomed cell (schematic, no molecular structures): glucose-analog tokens carrying glowing ¹⁸F tags enter and get trapped by hexokinase after step 1. Tokens accumulate inside a cluster labeled 'Tumor (schematic)' while ambient oxygen dots drift outside, and small radiation flashes travel from the trapped tokens to a detector ring drawn around the left torso silhouette (schematic), whose linked spot brightens into a warm PET hotspot.
scenes.narration: FDG-PET uses a glucose look-alike, or analog, labeled with radioactive fluorine-18. It is trapped after step 1, and the scanner detects its radiation. So tissues taking up glucose fast light up. Many tumors take up glucose fast even with oxygen present, the Warburg effect.

scenes.tts: Picture a bright spot on a patient's F D G PET scan. Those cells are pulling in glucose fast. Predict: does that bright spot prove the tissue is a tumor?
scenes.caption: Picture a bright spot on a patient's FDG-PET scan. Those cells are pulling in glucose fast. Predict: does that bright spot prove the tissue is a tumor?
scenes.visual: Left torso silhouette holds the bright 'FDG-PET hotspot (schematic)'. Right zoomed window removes the tumor label and shows unlabeled cells pulling in tracer tokens beneath a crisp high-contrast question: 'Does a bright spot prove a tumor?'.
scenes.narration: Picture a bright spot on a patient's FDG-PET scan. Those cells are pulling in glucose fast. Predict: does that bright spot prove the tissue is a tumor?

scenes.visual: Hold the question 'Does a bright spot prove a tumor?' on screen for 4.5 seconds while the torso hotspot pulses gently and tracer tokens drift slowly into the zoomed cell (schematic).

scenes.tts: No: F D G PET reports glucose uptake, not cancer itself. Inflamed tissue also takes up glucose fast. In a cold adult, heat-making brown fat can light up on PET C T too.
scenes.caption: No: FDG-PET reports glucose uptake, not cancer itself. Inflamed tissue also takes up glucose fast. In a cold adult, heat-making brown fat can light up on PET-CT too.
scenes.visual: The question flips to 'No: fast glucose uptake'. Right zoomed window splits along the same cell frame into 'Inflamed tissue (schematic)' and 'Brown fat in cold (schematic)' as both trap glowing tracer; on the left silhouette, neck-and-shoulder spots brighten with label 'PET-CT'.
scenes.narration: No: FDG-PET reports glucose uptake, not cancer itself. Inflamed tissue also takes up glucose fast. In a cold adult, heat-making brown fat can light up on PET-CT too.

scenes.tts: Other PET tracers track enzymes or protein deposits in living brains. In patients with probable Alzheimer disease, PET showed the drug donepezil cutting cortical acetylcholinesterase activity. That enzyme breaks down acetylcholine. That measures mechanism, not clinical benefit. The guiding idea: PET maps living chemistry, not whether a person benefits.

scenes.tts: The glucose-analog idea unlocked three findings. In 1988, Tootell and colleagues mapped macaque visual cortex, V one, with two-deoxyglucose, which marks active cells. Near the fovea, the centre of gaze, about fifteen millimetres of cortex served each degree. Estimates vary by animal and method, so fifteen is a macaque value.
scenes.caption: The glucose-analog idea unlocked three findings. In 1988, Tootell and colleagues mapped macaque visual cortex, V1, with 2-deoxyglucose, which marks active cells. Near the fovea, the centre of gaze, about 15 millimetres of cortex served each degree. Estimates vary by animal and method, so 15 is a macaque value.
scenes.visual: Right window transforms into a schematic strip of macaque 'V1 cortex' linked to a patterned target: '2-deoxyglucose' lights up active cells, stretching widest near 'Fovea' with a schematic bar labeled '~15 mm of cortex per degree (macaque value)'.

scenes.tts: In 1994, Luc Pellerin and Pierre Magistretti gave glutamate to cultured mouse astrocytes, glial cells. The cells took up more two-deoxyglucose and released more lactate. Blocking the sodium pump with ouabain blocked this. Their explanation: glutamate arrives with sodium, and pumping it out costs A T P, which drives glycolysis. They proposed that the lactate fuels active neurons.
scenes.caption: In 1994, Luc Pellerin and Pierre Magistretti gave glutamate to cultured mouse astrocytes, glial cells. The cells took up more 2-deoxyglucose and released more lactate. Blocking the sodium pump with ouabain blocked this. Their explanation: glutamate arrives with sodium, and pumping it out costs ATP, which drives glycolysis. They proposed that the lactate fuels active neurons.
scenes.visual: Right window zooms onto a schematic 'Astrocyte' beside a 'Neuron': 'Glutamate' enters with 'Na+', and '2-deoxyglucose' uptake and 'Lactate' release both rise; a red 'Ouabain' bar halts the 'Sodium pump' and the rise stops. Then the explanation chain appears as a tag: 'Na+ in → pump uses ATP → glycolysis' ('proposed').

scenes.tts: Finally, the 2023 A four study tracked amyloid, a plaque protein, for two hundred forty weeks. Adults with elevated amyloid got an antibody, solanezumab, or placebo. Amyloid PET uses centiloids: zero is the average plaque-free young adult, one hundred is typical Alzheimer dementia. Amyloid rose eleven point six centiloids with drug, nineteen point three with placebo.
scenes.caption: Finally, the 2023 A4 study tracked amyloid, a plaque protein, for 240 weeks. Adults with elevated amyloid got an antibody, solanezumab, or placebo. Amyloid PET uses centiloids: 0 is the average plaque-free young adult, 100 is typical Alzheimer dementia. Amyloid rose 11.6 centiloids with drug, 19.3 with placebo.
scenes.visual: Callout highlights the brain on the left silhouette (schematic). Right panel draws a computed 'Centiloid' axis from 0 ('Young adults, no plaques: average') to 100 ('Typical Alzheimer dementia: average'), and over '240 weeks' two computed bars climb to +11.6 ('Solanezumab') and +19.3 ('Placebo').
scenes.narration: Finally, the 2023 A4 study tracked amyloid, a plaque protein, for 240 weeks. Adults with elevated amyloid got an antibody, solanezumab, or placebo. Amyloid PET uses centiloids: 0 is the average plaque-free young adult, 100 is typical Alzheimer dementia. Amyloid rose 11.6 centiloids with drug, 19.3 with placebo.

scenes.tts: Subtract eleven point six from nineteen point three, then divide by nineteen point three. That equals about zero point four zero, or forty percent slower buildup. Yet a slower-rising imaging measure is not slower decline in the person. PET maps chemistry; benefit needs other proof.
scenes.caption: Subtract 11.6 from 19.3, then divide by 19.3. That equals about 0.40, or 40% slower buildup. Yet a slower-rising imaging measure is not slower decline in the person. PET maps chemistry; benefit needs other proof.
scenes.visual: Below the computed centiloid bars, the equation builds piece by piece as spoken: '(19.3 − 11.6) / 19.3 ≈ 0.40' and '~40% slower buildup'. A bold tag shows 'Slower amyloid rise ≠ slower decline', then the frame pulls back to the full glowing body silhouette and cell window (schematic).
